en: The Sūtra of King Suvarṇavarṇa, translated by the Indian Upāsaka Gautama Prajñāruci during the Eastern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, the Blessed One was dwelling together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, many bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās; various kings, royal ministers, and counselors; diverse followers of external paths, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, parivrājakas; as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, were attending upon him, making offerings, and honoring him with reverence, providing all that he required.

The World-Honored One has thus obtained great pure gains—robes, food, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and all manner of articles for the enjoyment of devas and humans—yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is neither stained nor attached by them, just as a lotus flower remains unsullied when in the water. His supreme and virtuous fame is heard throughout the world, and he is praised by all.

At that time, the World-Honored One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidvān, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—knowing what was appropriate for the occasion among all the worlds of gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, preached the Dharma as was fitting.

The Dharma he taught was good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it was excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, entirely complete, pure, and the pristine white Brahma-faring.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."

If there are sentient beings who can understand the fruit and the ripening of giving—just as I understand the fruit and the ripening of giving—and when eating their food, whether it be the first morsel or the last morsel, they do not eat without first setting aside a small portion to give away; being free from the defilement of envy, they are able to practice such giving.

"O monks! If there are sentient beings who do not know of giving, nor of the fruits, portions, and retributions of giving—as I know the fruits, portions, and retributions of giving—such beings, whether eating the first morsel or the last morsel, do not set aside even a small portion to give to others but instead eat it themselves; because they possess the defilement of envy, they are unable to give."
Why is this? O bhikṣus!

In the past there was a king named Suvarṇavarṇa (Golden Color), who was exceptionally handsome and distinguished, endowed with perfect physical features, and possessed a most supreme and wondrous body.

That King Suvarṇavarṇa was exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing vast treasures and many diverse goods, as well as many articles for enjoyment. He had abundant money, grain, pearls, and genuine pearls; he possessed many *kaśarva* gems and coral; he had much gold and silver, and an abundance of native gold. He owned many elephants and horses, and his stables were filled with numerous herds of cattle and mares.
The capital city of King Golden Color was named Abundant Gold City (Suvarṇaprabhāsa), where the king resided.

The city measured twelve yojanas in length from east to west and seven yojanas in width from south to north; it was filled with people so densely that there was no empty space between them, and it was peaceful, secure, and prosperous.
There were five billion seven hundred million villages and hamlets, filled with people who lived in peace, security, abundance, and joy;
there were sixty thousand mountains and rivers, all of which had great cities with rulers, filled with people who lived in peace, security, abundance, and joy.
That King Suvarṇavarṇa had a great retinue of eighteen thousand ministers and twenty thousand ladies of the inner palace.
That King Suvarṇavarṇa was well-versed in the laws of kingship and acted in accordance with them; he ruled as king over that kingdom in conformity with the law.
That King Kanakavarṇa was able to relinquish all that he possessed; there was nothing he would not give away, even his own body and flesh.
At that time, the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years.
At another time, King Suvarṇavarṇa, while dwelling in a secluded place in quiet contemplation, gave rise to this thought:
"I shall exempt all merchants from taxes, and I shall not impose levies upon any of my subjects."
At that time, King Golden, having reflected thus, summoned his great ministers, attendants, and all the officials of the various departments, both internal and external, and issued this decree:
"From this day forward, no taxes or duties shall be levied upon any of the people or any merchants; throughout the entire Jambudvīpa, all subjects are granted exemption from their taxes."
By these means, King Suvarṇavarṇa governed the kingdom according to the Dharma for many years.
Later, at another time, an evil star appeared, which was to cause the heavens not to rain for twelve years.
There was a brahmin well-versed in the art of physiognomy, proficient in the treatises on mantras, and knowledgeable regarding the movements and degrees of the planets, such as Venus.

Having observed an inauspicious star and having determined its significance through divination, he went to King Kanakavarṇa. Upon arriving at the king’s presence, he explained everything to the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should know that an evil star has now appeared; it is an ill omen for Your Majesty, and for twelve years the heavens shall not send down rain."
At that time, having heard these words, King Suvarṇavarṇa wept and shed tears, wailing and lamenting, and spoke thus:
"Alas for these people of my Jambudvīpa! How bitter it is!"
Alas! These people of my Jambudvīpa!
How could it be that this land of mine, Jambudvīpa—so peaceful, prosperous, and abundant with people—should, before long, become desolate and devoid of inhabitants?
Then, King Suvarṇavarṇa, having ceased his weeping after a brief moment, reflected thus:
"A wealthy man with abundant riches and an ample store of grain can survive for twelve years without dying."
"If those who are poor possess such meager wealth and lack sufficient grain for food, how shall they survive?
How will they be able to pass through these twelve years?
Having thought thus, King Kanakavarṇa reflected further and gave rise to this thought:
"I shall now gather all the grain and food within Jambudvīpa and pile it together in one place:

all from the outlying dwellings, all from the villages, all from the cities, all from the human settlements, and all from the territories of the kings—bringing forth every bit of grain and making it known in its quantity, I shall construct a granary in a single location."
"I shall calculate the number of inhabitants throughout Jambudvīpa and provide them with food equally for twelve years.

Having thought thus, King Suvarṇavarṇa immediately summoned his ministers, his attendants, the various officials of the inner and outer departments, and all the masters of the frontier guards and watchtowers; they all assembled, and he commanded them:
"Go forth and collect all the grain and provisions within Jambudvīpa, and measure to determine their quantity."

Upon hearing King Suvarṇavarṇa’s command, all those ministers throughout Jambudvīpa—in every outer residence, every village, every city, every inhabited place, and every royal domain—collected all the grain and provisions within Jambudvīpa and measured their quantities.

All the grain and food found throughout Jambudvīpa—in all outer dwellings, all villages, all cities, all inhabited places, and all royal territories—shall be brought together to a single location and made into a granary.
Thereafter, he went to where King Suvarṇa was and spoke these words:

"Your Majesty, you should now know that all the grain and food found in all the outer dwellings, all the villages, all the towns, all the inhabited places, and all the royal territories within Jambudvīpa have already been gathered together and their quantity has been measured."

All the grain and food found throughout Jambudvīpa—in all outer dwellings, all villages, all cities, all human settlements, and all royal domains—has already been brought together and stored in a single granary.
"Your Majesty should know the time; act as you please.
Then, King Suvarṇavarṇa summoned those in Jambudvīpa who were skilled in calculation and proficient in writing, and commanded them thus:
"Go now and quickly count the population of all the people within Jambudvīpa to determine their total number."
"Starting with myself, all the people within Jambudvīpa shall be given food equally; let everyone receive their portion.
Having heard King Suvarṇavarṇa’s command, those who were skilled in calculation and proficient in writing immediately departed in haste.

Having completed a full enumeration of all the people within Jambudvīpa and having ascertained their total number, those skilled in writing have prepared a formal document and respectfully submitted it to the King.

"At that time, King Golden himself, at the head of all the people within Jambudvīpa, provided food equally to everyone; he gave it sparingly, yet in this manner they survived without dying for eleven years."
"After eleven years have passed and one month has elapsed, there will be many men and women everywhere—whether male or female—who gradually suffer from hunger. Why is this?"

Because the grain was nearly exhausted, there were still eleven months remaining; yet in many places, there were many men and women—whether male or female—who were so hungry and thirsty they were on the verge of death.
"At that time, all grain and food throughout Jambudvīpa had been completely exhausted, and the storehouses were entirely empty.
At that moment, there remained only five measures of cooked rice, sufficient for one person's meal for a single day; this was the sole remaining portion of King Suvarṇavarṇa’s own meal."

"At that time, there was a person who had already practiced the bodhisattva path for forty kalpas in the past; having arrived at this Sahā world, he saw two sentient beings—a mother and son—engaging in sexual intercourse together within a certain forest."
At that time, having seen this, the Bodhisattva sighed in his heart, saying:
"How is it that such sentient beings harbor such extremely evil afflictions within their very flanks?
Having drunk her milk, they commit such deeds; where else could there be such an evil dharma?"

"I have no need for such beings; I have no need for such unrighteous beings—those people shrouded by unlawful desires, defilements, wrong views, and evil greed; those who do not recognize their parents, who do not know śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, who do not protect their lineage, who do not respect their elders, and who do not cherish their kin. I have no need now to benefit such extremely wicked beings; rather, I shall now practice the path to enlightenment for my own benefit."
At that time, having given rise to this thought, the Bodhisattva immediately went to another place, beneath the root of a different tree.
Having arrived there, he sat cross-legged at the foot of that tree, holding his body erect and maintaining right mindfulness.
At that time, that bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates of clinging in accordance with their emergence and subsidence:

"This is the arising of form; this is the dispersal and cessation of form. Likewise, he contemplates: "This is the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is the dispersal and cessation of consciousness."

In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates the five aggregates of clinging in accordance with reality; having seen their disappearance, before long, all conditioned phenomena that had accumulated disperse and perish.
Having understood it thus, by this cause and condition he immediately attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Having attained enlightenment, he spoke these verses:
"Because of craving, suffering arises; Thus one should abandon craving.
One should delight in dwelling alone, Like the single horn of the rhinoceros."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One of the Pratyekabuddhas, reflected thus:
"For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have practiced many austerities, yet not a single sentient being has received my benefit."
"Today, out of compassion for sentient beings and for their benefit, from whom shall I receive food and drink?
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One, having attained the supernormal power of the divine eye, which is pure and surpasses that of humans, surveyed the entire region of Jambudvīpa.

That Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One, saw that all food in Jambudvīpa had been exhausted, with only the single meal of five *śoṇa* measures of rice remaining for King Suvarṇa. Having observed this, he gave rise to this thought:
"Out of compassion for King Suvarṇa and to bring him benefit, I shall now go and take King Suvarṇa’s single meal and eat it."

Then the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One, immediately flew through the air by means of his supernormal powers, manifesting his body so that people could see him; with supernormal power like that of the Śakunī bird, he headed toward the capital city of Suvarṇapura, the Golden City, belonging to King Suvarṇa.
At that time, King Suvarṇavarṇa was staying upon his palace tower, and all five thousand ministers beheld that Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One.
Among those ministers, there was one who first saw from afar that Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One, as he was gradually approaching from a distance.
Having seen this, he spoke thus to the other ministers: "Look, all of you! Look, all of you!
From that distance, a red-winged *śāri* bird is coming toward us."
The second minister, having looked, replied:
"Your Majesty, observe closely!
That is not a red-winged śāri bird; it is a rākṣasa, an evil spirit who feeds on strength, wishing to come here to consume our power, and now it comes to devour me."
At that time, the minister showed [the bird] to King Kanakavarṇa and spoke thus.
Then King Kanakavarṇa rubbed his face with both hands and gazed intently; having observed it closely, he said to the minister:
"Minister, you should know that this is neither a red-winged śāri-karavi bird nor a rākṣasa demon of predatory strength; it is a ṛṣi who has come here out of compassion for me."
Then, in an instant, the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One of Solitary Awakening, arrived at the upper story of the palace where King Suvarṇavarṇa resided.

Upon seeing the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One of Solitary Awakening, King Suvarṇavarṇa immediately rose to greet him and prostrated at his feet. Having prostrated at his feet, he prepared excellent seating and invited him to take his seat.
When that Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One of the Pratyekabuddhas, had taken his seat, King Kanakavarṇa addressed the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One of the Pratyekabuddhas, saying:
"I wonder, O Seer, for what reason have you come here?"
He replied, "Great King! I have come here now for the sake of food."
When King Golden heard these words, he immediately wept with grief and said through his tears:
"How could I have expected to be so impoverished as this?"
"In this Jambudvīpa, I have already attained wealth, happiness, and self-mastery; yet now, this one seer is unable to provide me with even a single meal of fine food."
At that time, there was a certain goddess dwelling in the royal capital of Abhirūpa-kanaka who addressed King Kanakavarṇa in verse:
“What phenomenon is called suffering? What phenomenon is called happiness?”
What is it that is called poverty? Of what suffering is it the heaviest?
It is the suffering of poverty.
The suffering of death and the suffering of poverty—these two sufferings are equal and no different.
"It would be better to undergo the suffering of death than to live in poverty.
When King Suvarṇavarṇa heard these words, he summoned his chief cook and asked him:
"Do you have any food?"
"I wish to make an offering to this great seer.
The cook replied, "Your Majesty should know that all the grain and food in Jambudvīpa have been completely exhausted; there remains only a single meal for Your Majesty to eat."
At that time, King Golden thought to himself:
"If I eat [the flesh], my life will be preserved for a short while; if I do not eat it, my life will quickly end.
Having reflected thus, he further considered another thought:
"If I were to eat, I would still not escape death; if I do not eat, death will come to me as well.

I shall not seek such a meager life. This great seer maintains pure precepts and practices wholesome dharmas; since he has come to my home, how could I allow him to leave with an empty bowl, having received no food?"
At that time, King Suvarṇavarṇa, having reflected thus, commanded his great ministers, the officials of the various departments—both internal and external—and his retinue, saying:
"All of you should rejoice together!"

"This is the final act of giving by me, King Golden; by this root of merit, I pray that all the people of Jambudvīpa, from this day forward and into future lives, may forever sever the bonds of poverty."

Then, King Suvarṇavarṇa, having made this aspiration, took a single meal of rice and placed it within the alms-bowl held by the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One; having thus placed it there, he offered it into the right palm of the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One.

“At that time, such is the nature of the Dharma for Pratyekabuddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle: they demonstrate the Dharma through their bodies rather than by verbal explanation.

Then, having accepted the food offered by King Suvarṇavarṇa, the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, immediately departed through the air by means of his supernormal powers.”
At that time, King Suvarṇavarṇa and the entire great assembly all joined their palms and gazed intently with unblinking eyes until [the object] passed beyond the range of vision.
At that time, King Golden commanded his various ministers, the officials of all departments—both internal and external—and the gatekeepers and their retinues, speaking these words:
"All of you, depart; each shall go to your own home and die of hunger and thirst."
Those ministers, along with their retinues and all others, all said:
"O Lord, when there is the time for victory and joy, we shall all follow you, delighting in play and excursions, and together enjoy every pleasure."
"How can I now abandon the heavens and depart?

At that time, King Golden, having heard these words, wept with tears of sorrow. Wiping his tears with his hand, he spoke to his ministers, the officials of the various departments both internal and external, and his kinsmen, saying:
"All of you, depart each to your own homes, so that no one within my palace shall die of hunger and thirst."

At that time, the great ministers, the attendants, the officials of all departments both internal and external, and their kinsmen—all wept with piteous cries and shed tears. Having wiped away their tears with their hands, they proceeded together forward to approach King Suvarṇavarṇa.

Having arrived at the King’s presence, he prostrated himself with his head at the feet of King Suvarṇavarṇa. After paying homage at the King’s feet, he joined his palms together and addressed King Suvarṇavarṇa in this way:
"Whatever evil deeds I have committed, however many or few they may be, I pray only that Your Majesty will forgive me for these matters; I shall see Your Majesty for the last time this morning."

At that time, when the Pratyekabuddha, the World-Honored One, had accepted the offered food and was proceeding toward another place to eat it, four clouds arose simultaneously in the four directions; cool winds blew and fanned them, causing the ground throughout Jambudvīpa to become completely pure.

At that time, a cool breeze blew over Jambudvīpa; once the ground had been purified, for the latter half of the day, the heavens rained down various kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods) and *bhojaniya* (soft foods), such as these colored foods:
namely, rice, parched grain, and cooked beans; and such *bhojaniya* and *khādaniya* foods as cakes, roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, sesame seeds, and so forth.
Such solid foods (khādaniya) as these, furthermore, include oily substances and sweet cakes; such solid foods as rice-flour cakes, and various other kinds of food like those falling from the heavens.

At that time, King Golden saw these events and his heart was filled with great joy; he leaped for immeasurable delight, and a virtuous mind arose within him. He spoke thus to his various ministers, the officials of the inner and outer departments, his hundreds of subordinate officers, and his kinsmen:
"Look, all of you! Look, all of you!"
"By giving a single meal such as this to the morning sun, one obtains such a reward; furthermore, there are immeasurable other fruits of retribution that will surely be obtained hereafter.

When he had finished speaking thus, from the second day through the seventh day, various other kinds of grains rained down, namely: sesame, black beans, small beans, large wheat, small wheat, mung beans, vetch, rice, millet, and paddy.

After seven days of rain, in this same sequence, it rained clarified butter for seven days, oil for seven days, coins for seven days, and cotton cloth for seven days; furthermore, various mixed rains fell.

Then, for another seven days, there fell only the seven precious gems—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), crystal (*sphaṭika*), red pearls, as well as agate and musāragalva—these being the seven such jewels.
“O bhikṣus! You should know that through the cause and condition of King Suvarṇavarṇa’s gift of food, the poverty of all the people throughout Jambudvīpa was forever eliminated.”
“Monks, what do you think? Was that King Suvarṇavarṇa of the past someone else?
Do not view it thus. Why is that?
"O bhikṣus! That King Suvarṇavarṇa of the past was none other than myself. O bhikṣus!"

This gate is thus; you should understand it well. When such beings know the fruit of giving and the specific retribution for acts of giving—just as I know the fruits and specific retributions of giving—they do not eat even the first morsel or the last morsel without having first relinquished a small portion in charity; free from the stain of envy, they are able to practice generosity.

In this way, sentient beings do not know the fruit of giving or the partial recompense for acts of generosity—just as I know the fruit of giving and its partial recompense. When such beings eat their first morsel or their last morsel, they do not set aside even a small portion to give to others, but instead consume it themselves; because they are defiled by the stain of envy, they are unable to practice giving.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Whatever wholesome or unwholesome deeds were performed in the past, The karma of sin and merit is never lost.
By associating with those who are wise, The karma of coming and going is not lost."
Among the noble assembly, one speaks well; one does not fail in the karma of speech.
One who knows gratitude and repays kindness does not fail in the karma of action.
Good karma results in physical excellence; unwholesome karma results in ugliness.
"Both types of karma have retribution; they will certainly and truly yield their fruits.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the entire assembly—comprising the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—hearing what the Buddha had said, all rejoiced greatly.
The Sūtra of King Suvarṇavarṇa: A Record of its Translation. Śākyamuni Tathāgata has had immeasurable past lives; for instance, at one time, he was King Suvarṇavarṇa.

Through the causes and conditions of the practice of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), one attains Buddhahood by oneself; thus, the Dharma-gate of generosity is taught and that [king] is cited as a witness. For this reason, this sutra is titled "The Golden-Colored King" (*Suvarṇavarṇa-rāja*).

The Minister of the Secretariat of the Wei Dynasty, the Duke Gao of Yitong, possessing a heart of profound sincerity, went to Qi and obtained this golden manuscript. He opened this gateway to reveal it universally to all, and from the upper surface of his majestic residence, he brought forth this wondrous scripture.

The śramaṇas Tanlin and Gautama Liuqi translated this in the fourth year of the Xinghe era, when the year was Renxu, the lunar month was in You, the first day of the moon was Yiwei, on the day Guichou, completing the work on the day Yimao.
Three thousand five hundred and fourteen characters.
